title: Power Transformer
abstract:
Where the Function Transformer applies a rule you chose, the Power
Transformer learns the right transform from the data. It is an adaptive
transformer that estimates a parameter $\lambda$, and the two members of the
family are Box-Cox (requires strictly positive values) and Yeo-Johnson (an
extension that also handles zero and negative values). This document derives both
formulas, shows how $\lambda$ is estimated by maximum likelihood, explains why
$\lambda=0$ recovers the log transform exactly, and covers the Quantile
Transformer as the non-parametric alternative.

blocks.t: The Idea
From the notes

An adaptive transformer that learns $\lambda$ from the data. In the
Function Transformer we chose $\lambda$; here it learns.

In Topic 18 you looked at a histogram, decided the skew was positive, and picked
$\log$. That is a guess from a menu of five options. The Power Transformer
replaces the menu with a continuous family indexed by a single parameter
$\lambda$, and then estimates the $\lambda$ that makes the transformed column as
close to normal as possible.

blocks.cap:
Left: the Box-Cox family for several values of $\lambda$. One formula
 contains the reciprocal ($\lambda=-1$), the log ($\lambda=0$), the square root
 ($\lambda=0.5$), the identity ($\lambda=1$) and the square ($\lambda=2$).
 Right: the profile log-likelihood, whose maximum defines $\hat\lambda$.

blocks.t: Box-Cox Transform
From the notes

All values are strictly positive, $X>0$. Produces the
most normal possible distribution with the best $\lambda$.
Range searched: $(-5,5)$.
The formula
Why the $\lambda=0$ case is $\ln x$ and not a special case

The two branches look like an arbitrary patch. They are not — the second is the
limit of the first.
The limit
Write $x^{\lambda}=e^{\lambda\ln x}$ and expand for small $\lambda$:
x^{\lambda}=1+\lambda\ln x+\frac{(\lambda\ln x)^2}{2!}+\cdots
Therefore

So the family is continuous in $\lambda$, and the log is simply the
member at $\lambda=0$. Subtracting the $1$ and dividing by $\lambda$ exists
precisely to make this limit work; without them the family would collapse to the
constant $1$ at $\lambda=0$.
Everything in Topic 18 is a point in this family

The log, square root, reciprocal and square transforms are all members. The Power
Transformer's contribution is that it does not force you to land on a round
number — it may find $\hat\lambda = 0.137$, which no manual menu offers.
How $\lambda$ is estimated
Maximum likelihood

Assume $x^{(\lambda)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$. The log-likelihood, after
profiling out $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$, reduces to

\ell(\lambda)= -\frac{n}{2}\ln \left(\hat\sigma^2_{\lambda}\right)
 +(\lambda-1)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln x_i ,

where $\hat\sigma^2_{\lambda}$ is the sample variance of the transformed data.
The estimate is $\hat\lambda=\arg\max_\lambda \ell(\lambda)$, found by a
one-dimensional numerical search over $(-5,5)$.

The second term, $(\lambda-1)\sum\ln x_i$, is the Jacobian of the
transformation. Without it the optimiser would simply shrink the data towards
zero variance and report a meaningless $\lambda$; the Jacobian penalises that,
because the likelihood must be a density on the original scale.
$\lambda$ is a learned parameter, so it is fitted on train only

$\hat\lambda$ is estimated from data exactly like a mean or a category list. Fit
the transformer on the training set and reuse the same $\hat\lambda$ on test.
Re-estimating on test would put the two sets on different scales.
Yeo-Johnson Transform
From the notes

An extension of the Box-Cox transform. It works for negative and
zero values, unlike the Box-Cox transformer.
The formula

\boxed{ 
 x_i^{(\lambda)}=
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{(x_i+1)^{\lambda}-1}{\lambda}, & \lambda\neq0, x_i\ge0,
[9pt]
 \ln(x_i+1), & \lambda=0, x_i\ge0,
[9pt]
 -\dfrac{(-x_i+1)^{2-\lambda}-1}{2-\lambda}, & \lambda\neq2, x_i<0,
[9pt]
 -\ln(-x_i+1), & \lambda=2, x_i<0.
 \end{cases} }

The construction is easier to read than it looks. For $x\ge0$ it is Box-Cox
applied to $x+1$, which shifts the domain so that zero is allowed. For $x<0$ it
reflects the value, applies the same idea with the exponent $2-\lambda$, and
reflects the result back — so the function is continuous and monotone
increasing across the whole real line, and smooth at $x=0$. A single $\lambda$
governs both halves.

blocks.cap:
The one distinction that decides which you use. Box-Cox raises an error
 on data containing negative values; Yeo-Johnson handles it.

head: Box-Cox
Yeo-Johnson
rows: Strictly positive data — price, income, area
Anything else, or when you are unsure

blocks.t: Yeo-Johnson is the safe default

It is scikit-learn's default for good reason: it never fails on the domain, and on
strictly positive data it produces results very close to Box-Cox. Choose Box-Cox
when the data is guaranteed positive and you want the slightly better-established
statistical properties.
Standardize After

Both transformers in scikit-learn have standardize=True by default, which
applies a StandardScaler to the transformed output. This is usually what
you want — Box-Cox with $\lambda=-1$ produces values in a strange range — but
be aware it is happening, because it means the output has mean 0 and standard
deviation 1 and you do not need a separate scaling step.
Quantile Transformer

The third scikit-learn transformer named in the notes' diagram. It is the
non-parametric alternative: instead of fitting a parametric family, it maps each
value to its rank, converts the rank to a quantile, and pushes that
quantile through the inverse CDF of a target distribution (normal or uniform).

blocks.cap:
The whole family on one column. The Power Transformers find a
 near-perfect $\lambda$; the Quantile Transformer forces normality by
 construction — note its skew is essentially zero regardless of the input.

head: Power Transformer
Quantile Transformer
rows: Erases them — they become ordinary quantiles
Needs enough rows to estimate quantiles
Can destroy genuine signal in the tails; distorts distances

blocks.t: The Quantile Transformer is a blunt instrument

It will make any distribution normal, including one that is bimodal
because it contains two genuinely different populations. That flattening
discards information a model might have used. It also makes the transform
sensitive to the training sample — new values outside the observed range are
clipped to the extremes. Reach for it when the Power Transformer has failed, not
first.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.preprocessing import (PowerTransformer, QuantileTransformer,
                                   StandardScaler, FunctionTransformer)
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline, Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.lognormal(3.0, .8, 5000).reshape(-1, 1)

# =====================================================================
# 1. BOX-COX -- it LEARNS lambda instead of you guessing
# =====================================================================
bc = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox", standardize=True).fit(x)
print("learned lambda:", bc.lambdas_.round(4))       # e.g. [0.0132]
xb = bc.transform(x)
print(f"skew  before {stats.skew(x.ravel()):+.3f}  after {stats.skew(xb.ravel()):+.3f}")

# lambda ~ 0 means the data wanted a LOG. Compare:
print("log skew      :", round(stats.skew(np.log(x.ravel())), 4))
print("box-cox skew  :", round(stats.skew(xb.ravel()), 4))   # usually better

# It is invertible:
print("round-trips:", np.allclose(bc.inverse_transform(xb), x))

# =====================================================================
# 2. lambda = 0 IS the log -- verify the limit numerically
# =====================================================================
v = np.array([2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 100.0])
for lam in [1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-6]:
    approx = (v ** lam - 1) / lam
    print(f"lambda={lam:<8} max |boxcox - ln| = {np.abs(approx - np.log(v)).max():.2e}")
# 1e-1 -> 2.7e+00 ... 1e-6 -> 2.7e-05 : it converges to ln(x).

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE MAXIMUM-LIKELIHOOD SEARCH, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
def boxcox_loglik(lam, d):
    n = len(d)
    z = np.log(d) if abs(lam) < 1e-9 else (d ** lam - 1) / lam
    return -n / 2 * np.log(z.var()) + (lam - 1) * np.log(d).sum()
    #                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the Jacobian term
    # Without it the optimiser just shrinks the variance to zero.

grid = np.linspace(-2, 2, 4001)
ll = np.array([boxcox_loglik(l, x.ravel()) for l in grid])
print("scratch lambda :", round(grid[ll.argmax()], 4))
print("sklearn lambda :", round(bc.lambdas_[0], 4))
print("scipy   lambda :", round(stats.boxcox(x.ravel())[1], 4))    # all agree

# =====================================================================
# 4. BOX-COX FAILS ON NON-POSITIVE DATA
# =====================================================================
mixed = np.r_[rng.normal(-3, 2, 1500), rng.lognormal(1.2, .7, 2500)].reshape(-1, 1)
print("min value:", mixed.min().round(2))            # negative

try:
    PowerTransformer(method="box-cox").fit(mixed)
except ValueError as e:
    print("Box-Cox refuses:", str(e)[:70])

yj = PowerTransformer(method="yeo-johnson").fit(mixed)   # works
print("Yeo-Johnson lambda:", yj.lambdas_.round(4),
      "skew after:", round(stats.skew(yj.transform(mixed).ravel()), 3))

# Zeros break Box-Cox too:
withzero = np.array([[0.], [1.], [5.], [20.]])
try:
    PowerTransformer(method="box-cox").fit(withzero)
except ValueError as e:
    print("zeros also refused:", str(e)[:50])
print("Yeo-Johnson handles zeros:",
      PowerTransformer(method="yeo-johnson").fit_transform(withzero).ravel().round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE WHOLE FAMILY, COMPARED
# =====================================================================
qt = QuantileTransformer(output_distribution="normal",
                         n_quantiles=1000, random_state=0)
variants = {
    "original":     x.ravel(),
    "log":          np.log(x.ravel()),
    "sqrt":         np.sqrt(x.ravel()),
    "box-cox":      bc.transform(x).ravel(),
    "yeo-johnson":  PowerTransformer("yeo-johnson").fit_transform(x).ravel(),
    "quantile":     qt.fit_transform(x).ravel(),
}
for name, v in variants.items():
    _, p = stats.normaltest(v)
    print(f"{name:13s} skew {stats.skew(v):+7.4f}  kurt {stats.kurtosis(v):+7.3f}  "
          f"normaltest p={p:.2e}")
# quantile always wins on skew -- because it FORCES normality by construction.

# =====================================================================
# 6. DOES IT HELP THE MODEL? (and beware: the quantile transformer can hurt)
# =====================================================================
n = 5000
inc = rng.lognormal(10.5, .9, n)
age = rng.uniform(20, 65, n)
y = (0.4 * np.log(inc) + 0.05 * age + rng.normal(0, .8, n) > 5.2).astype(int)
X = np.c_[inc, age]

setups = {
    "raw + scale":    make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    "log + scale":    make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(np.log1p), StandardScaler(),
                                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    "yeo-johnson":    make_pipeline(PowerTransformer(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    "box-cox":        make_pipeline(PowerTransformer(method="box-cox"),
                                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    "quantile":       make_pipeline(QuantileTransformer(output_distribution="normal",
                                                        random_state=0),
                                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
}
for name, pipe in setups.items():
    s = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"{name:14s} cv auc {s.mean():.4f} +/- {s.std():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. FIT ON TRAIN ONLY -- lambda is a learned parameter
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te = train_test_split(x, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
pt = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox").fit(X_tr)   # lambda learned HERE
print("lambda from train:", pt.lambdas_.round(4))
X_te_t = pt.transform(X_te)                          # SAME lambda reused
print("test skew after:", round(stats.skew(X_te_t.ravel()), 4))

wrong = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox").fit_transform(X_te)   # DO NOT
print("re-fitted lambda on test (different scale!):",
      PowerTransformer(method="box-cox").fit(X_te).lambdas_.round(4))

# =====================================================================
# 8. PER-COLUMN LAMBDAS INSIDE A ColumnTransformer
# =====================================================================
df = pd.DataFrame({"income": inc, "age": age,
                   "score": rng.beta(6, 2, n) * 100})     # LEFT skewed
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("power", PowerTransformer(method="yeo-johnson"), ["income", "score"]),
    ("plain", StandardScaler(),                       ["age"]),
])
pre.fit(df)
lam = pre.named_transformers_["power"].lambdas_
print(dict(zip(["income", "score"], lam.round(3))))
# income ~0.0  (right skew -> log-like)   score ~1.9 (LEFT skew -> square-like)
# One transformer, opposite corrections, both learned automatically.
Worked Examples
Box-Cox on a right-skewed column
Values $x = [1,\,2,\,4,\,8]$ (a geometric sequence: each value doubles). Box-Cox: $x^{(\lambda)} = (x^\lambda - 1)/\lambda$ for $\lambda \ne 0$, and $\ln x$ for $\lambda = 0$.
Step 1 – skewness of the raw values. Sample skewness $= +0.657$: right-tailed, the 8 pulls the tail out.
Step 2 – $\lambda = 0.5$.
Step 3 – $\lambda = 0$ (log).

These are equally spaced: every step is $\ln 2 = 0.693$, so the skewness is $0.000$. The log turns a geometric progression into an arithmetic one, which is exactly what a symmetric distribution looks like.

Step 4 – how the fitted $\lambda$ is chosen. Scikit-learn's PowerTransformer finds the $\lambda$ that maximises the Gaussian log-likelihood of the transformed data. Here $\lambda=0$ is nearly optimal, so the data are log-normal-like. Because $\lambda$ is learned, the same code works without you guessing between log, square root and reciprocal.
Constraint. Box-Cox needs $x>0$. For zero or negative values use Yeo-Johnson. With $\lambda=0$ it maps $x\ge0$ to $\ln(x+1)$ and $x<0$ to $-\big[(1-x)^{2}-1\big]/2$:
x=-2 \mapsto -4.000, \qquad x=0 \mapsto 0, \qquad x=2 \mapsto \ln 3 = 1.099
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
The Power Transformer is an adaptive transformer that learns
 $\lambda$ from the data. In the Function Transformer we chose
 $\lambda$; here it learns.

Box-Cox:
 $x^{(\lambda)}=\frac{x^{\lambda}-1}{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\neq0$, and
 $\ln x$ for $\lambda=0$. All values must be strictly positive
 ($X>0$). It finds the most normal possible distribution with the
 best $\lambda$, searched over $(-5,5)$.

The $\lambda=0$ branch is not a special case — it is the
 limit of the general formula, which is why the family is
 continuous.

$\lambda=-1$ is the reciprocal, $0$ the log, $0.5$ the square root, $1$
 the identity, $2$ the square. Every Topic 18 transform is a point in this
 family.

$\lambda$ is estimated by maximum likelihood, with a Jacobian
 term that prevents the optimiser from trivially shrinking the variance.

Yeo-Johnson is an extension of Box-Cox that
 works for negative and zero values. It is scikit-learn's default
 and the safe choice.
standardize=True is on by default — the output is already scaled.

The Quantile Transformer is the non-parametric alternative: it
 forces normality by rank, handles multimodality, and erases outliers —
 sometimes destroying real signal.
$\lambda$ is a learned parameter: fit on train only.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson — how do you choose?

By the domain of the data. Box-Cox requires strictly positive values;
Yeo-Johnson handles zeros and negatives. On strictly positive data they give
very similar results, so Yeo-Johnson is the safe default and Box-Cox the choice
when positivity is guaranteed.

Q. Why is Box-Cox defined as $\frac{x^\lambda-1}{\lambda}$ rather than
just $x^\lambda$?

So that the family is continuous at $\lambda=0$. Expanding
$x^\lambda = e^{\lambda\ln x}$ shows $\frac{x^\lambda-1}{\lambda}\to\ln x$ as
$\lambda\to0$. Plain $x^\lambda$ would collapse to the constant 1 and the log
would not be a member of the family.
Q. How is $\lambda$ chosen?

By maximum likelihood — a one-dimensional search maximising the profile
log-likelihood of the transformed data under a normal model, including a Jacobian
term $(\lambda-1)\sum\ln x_i$.

Q. The Power Transformer gave $\lambda\approx1$. What does that tell
you?

That the data is already close to normal and no transformation is needed
($\lambda=1$ is the identity, up to a shift). Do not force a transform.

Q. Should you use the Quantile Transformer instead — it always gives
perfect normality?

Usually no. It achieves normality by rank, which flattens genuinely multimodal
distributions, erases outliers that may be meaningful, distorts distances, and
clips unseen values to the observed range. Prefer a Power Transformer; use the
Quantile Transformer when that has failed.
Q. Do you still need a StandardScaler after a PowerTransformer?

No — standardize=True is the default, so the output already has mean 0
and standard deviation 1.
